currentContext.business: CIL mines and markets coal through seven wholly owned coal producing subsidiaries, the directly managed North Eastern Coalfields, and a mine planning and consultancy arm (CMPDIL), operating across India's major coal-bearing regions. It operates across the coal value chain with in-house exploration, mine planning, project development and mining operations, supplying primarily the power sector plus steel, cement and other industrial (non-regulated sector) consumers through FSAs and e-auctions. The Company is concurrently diversifying into renewable energy (solar, wind, BESS), thermal power JVs, coal gasification, critical minerals and rail evacuation infrastructure.

Consultancy: Mine planning, design and consultancy services (CMPDIL)

currentContext.expansion: Coal India's expansion programme runs on four tracks: core mining capacity, evacuation infrastructure, renewables/storage, and diversification into thermal, gasification and critical minerals. On mining, 124 ongoing coal projects costing more than H 20 Crores are under implementation as at 31st March 2026, with total capacity of 1,044.79 MTY and capital of H 1,69,452.25 Crores - 91 on schedule and 33 delayed, the primary bottlenecks being Forest Clearance, land acquisition/possession and R&R. During FY 2025-26 three coal mining projects were operationalised with 9.0 MTY capacity and a capital outlay of H 936.18 Crores; 13 new mining projects were approved with sanctioned capital of H 13,601.18 Crores and about 77 MTY capacity (about 22 MTY incremental), plus 3 non-mining rail projects with sanctioned capital of H 13,419.95 Crores. New production commenced at 2 MDO projects (20.00 MTY capacity, 1.75 MT produced) and 3 Revenue Sharing projects (4.46 MTY, 0.41 MT produced). The long-term roadmap targets approximately 1 Billion Tonne of coal production by FY 2029-30, supported by 29 identified MDO projects of 254.05 MTPA (Phase-I 15 projects / 172.67 MTPA, Phase-II 14 projects / 81.38 MTPA; 17 opencast and 12 underground), a UG vision of 50 MT from underground mines by 2029-30, at least 140 Continuous Miners by 2034-35, and highwall mining of idle open-cast mines (5 in operation, 4 under implementation, LoA issued for 3 expected to start in 2026-27). For FY 2026-27, EC for 8 proposals of about 21.45 Mty, Stage-II FC for 12 proposals covering 2,800.145 Ha of forest land and possession of about 4,171.79 Ha of land are the stated enablers. On evacuation, the First Mile Connectivity programme comprises 72 projects of 843.0 MTY planned capacity with an estimated investment of H 24,600 Crores (the Chairman's spread states H 25,600 Crores), split Phase I 33 projects/379.5 MTY, Phase II 8/55.0, Phase III 17/334.5, Phase IV 14/74.0, with 27 operational, 18 under construction and 27 under formulation/approval; 9 FMC projects of 58.5 MTY were completed during FY 2025-26, and the goal is to expand mechanised evacuation from 151 MTY to 994 MTY. Seven railway projects are under execution - two on deposit basis (Tori-Shivpur New BG Line, 44.37 KM, tripling commissioned March 2024, enabling about 100 MTY from North Karanpura/CCL; Jharsuguda-Barpali-Sardega, 52.41 KM, doubling commissioned February 2024, with flyover complex targeted December 2026 and loading bulbs July 2027 to enhance capacity to about 90 MTY) and five through JVs/SPVs (MCRL Angul-Balram 14.2 KM commissioned, about 15 MTY for MCL; JCRL Shivpur-Kathautia 49 KM at 68.5% progress, commissioning expected June 2027, about 25 MTY for CCL; CERL Phase-I East Rail Corridor 124.7 KM at 96%, balance work by December 2026, about 65 MTY for SECL; CERL Phase-II Dharamjaigarh-Urga 63 KM at 38%, commissioning expected March 2027; CEWRL Gevra Road-Pendra Road 135 KM at 80%, commissioning expected December 2026, about 65 MTY for SECL). Project governance has been digitised through the SAP Project System module, with all 124 ongoing mining projects live and integrated with CIL's ERP and the National Coal Portal and IIG-PMG portals. On renewables, installed capacity is 357.65 MW (rooftop 34.15 MW, ground-mounted 323.50 MW), with about 523.50 MW under execution expected by FY 2026-27, including the 300 MW Khavda solar project in Gujarat (200 MW commissioned as of July 2026), 223.50 MW under construction and about 344.25 MW under DPR/feasibility across BCCL, CCL, ECL, MCL, NCL, SECL and WCL. Rooftop solar saturation of 35.19 MW was achieved under PM Surya Ghar Yojana against an assigned target of 34.03 MW. A structured year-wise pathway takes progressive capacity to 1,338 MW by FY 2026-27, 3,103 MW by FY 2027-28, 8,954 MW by FY 2028-29 and 9,410 MW by FY 2029-30, against a committed 3,000 MW by FY 2027-28 internal net-zero target and about 9,500 MW by FY 2029-30. Delivery routes are JVs with state gencos (CIL Rajasthan Akshay Urja Limited with RRVUNL, including 875 MW at Pugal Solar Park; a proposed JV with UPRVUNL in Uttar Pradesh), tariff-based competitive bidding (600 MW awarded at Jalaun Solar Park via NHPC's TBCB), captive projects and C&I supply - including MoUs with C&I consumers for 4.5 GW of renewable power through wind-solar hybrid projects, with planned development of 1.5 GW wind and 3 GW solar. Storage is a new growth area with BESPAs signed for a total of 267.5 MW / 1,070 MWh (187.5 MW/750 MWh with TGGENCO in Telangana and 80 MW/320 MWh with GRIDCO in Odisha). A wind portfolio has been initiated in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, and a dedicated Renewable Energy Division at headquarters steers the programme with CMPDIL as project management consultant. In conventional power, a 50:50 JV with Damodar Valley Corporation will develop a 2 x 800 MW (1,600 MW) brownfield thermal plant at Chandrapura with an investment of H 21,000 Crores. Capacity utilisation in FY 2025-26 was 88% for opencast and 77% for underground mines, with approximately 2,462 million cubic metres of coal and overburden handled, and 2.20 MT of washed coking coal and 6.51 MT of washed non-coking coal produced through washeries.

risks.risk: Business risk from captive and commercial coal mining (Risk That Matter)
risks.note: CIL's near-monopoly on domestic coal is being eroded by captive and commercial miners. It is formally classified as a Risk That Matter and is also shown as a strategic 'Risk to Value Creation' in the value-creation model. Management's stated response is implementation of SHAKTI 2025, enabling imported-coal-based power plants to obtain domestic coal linkages, encouraging wider participation in coal auctions including foreign bidders, and customer-centric measures to enhance market competitiveness - i.e. defending share rather than pricing power.

risks.risk: Impact of Nationally Determined Commitments (NDCs) on coal demand and production (Risk That Matter)
risks.note: The energy-transition risk is explicitly on the RTM register: India's climate commitments could structurally cap or reverse coal demand. This is the existential risk for a single-commodity producer whose entire core business is thermal coal, and it is the stated rationale for the renewable, storage, gasification and critical-minerals diversification. The routed text is truncated mid-sentence exactly where management begins describing its response ('CIL continues to').

risks.risk: Delay in land acquisition and possession for mining projects, with cost implication for permanent employment (Risk That Matter)
risks.note: Land is the binding constraint on the 1 BT-by-FY30 roadmap: 4,171.79 Ha must be possessed by subsidiaries just to hit the FY 2026-27 target, and land/R&R delays are cited as a primary bottleneck behind 33 of 124 ongoing projects running late. The stated risk explicitly includes the cost consequence of the permanent-employment obligations attached to land acquisition, which converts a project delay into a structural cost burden.

risks.risk: Delay in obtaining statutory clearances (Risk That Matter)
risks.note: Environmental Clearance and Stage-II Forest Clearance gate incremental capacity - EC for 8 proposals of about 21.45 Mty and Stage-II FC for 12 proposals covering 2,800.145 Ha of forest land are required for the FY 2026-27 target alone. Forest Clearance delays are named as a primary bottleneck for delayed projects. Clearance timing is outside the Company's control and directly determines whether production targets are met.

Mining is described by management as an inherently complex business where safety remains the foremost priority. It carries both a human cost and the risk of mine stoppages and regulatory action. Mitigation is comprehensive safety audits of all producing mines, Principal Hazard Management Plans, mine-specific Safety Management Plans, Integrated Command and Control Centres across all producing subsidiaries and NEC, AI-enabled video analytics and a Safety AI Analytics Dashboard.

Listed first among the six RTMs and repeated in the SWOT threats and the value-creation risk map. CIL runs SAP as its system of record across mining projects and financial reporting, with an Online Reconciliation Portal integrating quantity, quality and finance data for external consumers, so a cyber event would hit operations, customer settlement and financial reporting simultaneously.

risks.risk: Risk of unviable underground mining operations (Non-RTM Major Risk)
risks.note: Structurally important because it collides with strategy: opencast mines contributed 96.67% of raw coal output in FY 2025-26 and opencastable coal is stated to be likely exhausted in the near future, forcing a shift to underground mining where a 50 MT-by-2029-30 vision plan and at least 140 Continuous Miners by 2034-35 are planned. Underground capacity utilisation was 77% versus 88% for opencast. The Company itself flags that these operations may be unviable.

risks.risk: Critical manpower and succession planning risk (Non-RTM Major Risk)
risks.note: Named as 'Inadequate Succession Planning leading to shortage of critical manpower' on the risk register and echoed in the SWOT weaknesses as 'ageing work force and skill attrition'. With 2,12,066 employees and a simultaneous need to staff renewable energy, storage and critical-minerals businesses, capability transition is a live constraint; mitigation is training, leadership programmes and lateral hiring.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: CIL mines and markets coal through seven wholly owned coal producing subsidiaries, the directly managed North Eastern Coalfields, and a mine planning and consultancy arm (CMPDIL), operating across India's major coal-bearing regions. It operates across the coal value chain with in-house exploration, mine planning, project development and mining operations, supplying primarily the power sector plus steel, cement and other industrial (non-regulated sector) consumers through FSAs and e-auctions. The Company is concurrently diversifying into renewable energy (solar, wind, BESS), thermal power JVs, coal gasification, critical minerals and rail evacuation infrastructure.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Coal remains India's most significant indigenous energy resource and a cornerstone of energy security, with abundant availability, cost-effectiveness and reliability making it a strategic asset for baseload power.
- As on 31st March 2026 India's coal-based power generation capacity is about 229 GW of a total installed capacity of about 533 GW, i.e. about 42% share, underscoring coal's continued indispensable role.
- Coal is poised to remain a dominant fuel in India's energy portfolio; as envisioned in the Vision @2047 roadmap coal remains pivotal. While growth in coal demand may moderate post-2035, absolute demand is expected to remain steady or increase, driven by sustained baseload requirements.
- Total geological coal resources in India are estimated at about 401 Billion Tonnes as on 1st April 2025 (Geological Survey of India); at the current rate of production the reserves are adequate to meet demand.
- Demand headwind in FY 2025-26: total power generation (incl. RES) grew only about 0.9% to about 1,844.5 BU, coal-based generation fell 3.7% to 1,250 BU and domestic coal-based generation fell 2.3% to 1,174.4 BU. Management describes market headwinds and moderation in coal demand growth.
- Materialisation gap on power-sector demand: FY 2025-26 power sector demand was 668 MT against which CIL supplied 588.01 MT, an 88% materialisation.
- Non-Regulated Sector supply reached 155.5 MT, up 7.0% and the highest NRS supply in any year - a mix shift toward higher-realisation non-power customers.
- E-auction volumes rose to 101.72 MT from 89.38 MT, but the e-auction premium narrowed to 46% from 48% - a realisation headwind despite higher volume.
- Long-term contracted demand base: FSA commitment for power, non-power and bridge linkage of about 793.90 MTPA as on 31.03.2026; SHAKTI and revised SHAKTI operative linkage of about 643.4 MTPA with power and 119.2 MTPA with non-power consumers.
- Ministry of Coal demand for CIL coal from the power sector for FY 2026-27 is 669.80 MT.
- New demand pools management intends to tap: more coking coal to the steel sector and coal supply to upcoming coal gasification projects.
- FY 2025-26 dispatch was constrained by incessant rainfall in Q2, railway evacuation constraints and rake availability - evacuation is the stated bottleneck being addressed.
- Cost/quality lever: declared-vs-analysed GCV gap of only 56.7 Kcal/kg and final grade conformity of 86% in FY 2025-26 support realisation and reduce disputes.
- Structural cost weakness flagged in SWOT: higher fixed cost and resultant cost of production; inherent inferior quality of indigenous coal due to high ash content; ageing workforce and skill attrition; absence of indigenous manufacturing support.
- Diversification is being framed as a growth platform - coal gasification, critical minerals, renewable energy, battery storage and power generation broaden the growth base alongside the core.
- CIL's initiatives are aligned to the national target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
- Fuel Supply Agreement (FSA) commitment for Power Sector, Non-Power and bridge linkage at about 793.90 Million Tonne Per Annum (MTPA) as on 31.03.2026.
- Operative SHAKTI / revised SHAKTI linkage of about 643.4 MTPA with the power sector and 119.2 MTPA with non-power consumers as on 31st March 2026.
- As on 1st April 2026, 124 ongoing mining projects costing H 20 Crores and above, of about 1,044.79 Mty capacity, with sanctioned capital of H 1,69,452.25 Crores, at different stages of implementation.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Coal India's expansion programme runs on four tracks: core mining capacity, evacuation infrastructure, renewables/storage, and diversification into thermal, gasification and critical minerals. On mining, 124 ongoing coal projects costing more than H 20 Crores are under implementation as at 31st March 2026, with total capacity of 1,044.79 MTY and capital of H 1,69,452.25 Crores - 91 on schedule and 33 delayed, the primary bottlenecks being Forest Clearance, land acquisition/possession and R&R. During FY 2025-26 three coal mining projects were operationalised with 9.0 MTY capacity and a capital outlay of H 936.18 Crores; 13 new mining projects were approved with sanctioned capital of H 13,601.18 Crores and about 77 MTY capacity (about 22 MTY incremental), plus 3 non-mining rail projects with sanctioned capital of H 13,419.95 Crores. New production commenced at 2 MDO projects (20.00 MTY capacity, 1.75 MT produced) and 3 Revenue Sharing projects (4.46 MTY, 0.41 MT produced). The long-term roadmap targets approximately 1 Billion Tonne of coal production by FY 2029-30, supported by 29 identified MDO projects of 254.05 MTPA (Phase-I 15 projects / 172.67 MTPA, Phase-II 14 projects / 81.38 MTPA; 17 opencast and 12 underground), a UG vision of 50 MT from underground mines by 2029-30, at least 140 Continuous Miners by 2034-35, and highwall mining of idle open-cast mines (5 in operation, 4 under implementation, LoA issued for 3 expected to start in 2026-27). For FY 2026-27, EC for 8 proposals of about 21.45 Mty, Stage-II FC for 12 proposals covering 2,800.145 Ha of forest land and possession of about 4,171.79 Ha of land are the stated enablers. On evacuation, the First Mile Connectivity programme comprises 72 projects of 843.0 MTY planned capacity with an estimated investment of H 24,600 Crores (the Chairman's spread states H 25,600 Crores), split Phase I 33 projects/379.5 MTY, Phase II 8/55.0, Phase III 17/334.5, Phase IV 14/74.0, with 27 operational, 18 under construction and 27 under formulation/approval; 9 FMC projects of 58.5 MTY were completed during FY 2025-26, and the goal is to expand mechanised evacuation from 151 MTY to 994 MTY. Seven railway projects are under execution - two on deposit basis (Tori-Shivpur New BG Line, 44.37 KM, tripling commissioned March 2024, enabling about 100 MTY from North Karanpura/CCL; Jharsuguda-Barpali-Sardega, 52.41 KM, doubling commissioned February 2024, with flyover complex targeted December 2026 and loading bulbs July 2027 to enhance capacity to about 90 MTY) and five through JVs/SPVs (MCRL Angul-Balram 14.2 KM commissioned, about 15 MTY for MCL; JCRL Shivpur-Kathautia 49 KM at 68.5% progress, commissioning expected June 2027, about 25 MTY for CCL; CERL Phase-I East Rail Corridor 124.7 KM at 96%, balance work by December 2026, about 65 MTY for SECL; CERL Phase-II Dharamjaigarh-Urga 63 KM at 38%, commissioning expected March 2027; CEWRL Gevra Road-Pendra Road 135 KM at 80%, commissioning expected December 2026, about 65 MTY for SECL). Project governance has been digitised through the SAP Project System module, with all 124 ongoing mining projects live and integrated with CIL's ERP and the National Coal Portal and IIG-PMG portals. On renewables, installed capacity is 357.65 MW (rooftop 34.15 MW, ground-mounted 323.50 MW), with about 523.50 MW under execution expected by FY 2026-27, including the 300 MW Khavda solar project in Gujarat (200 MW commissioned as of July 2026), 223.50 MW under construction and about 344.25 MW under DPR/feasibility across BCCL, CCL, ECL, MCL, NCL, SECL and WCL. Rooftop solar saturation of 35.19 MW was achieved under PM Surya Ghar Yojana against an assigned target of 34.03 MW. A structured year-wise pathway takes progressive capacity to 1,338 MW by FY 2026-27, 3,103 MW by FY 2027-28, 8,954 MW by FY 2028-29 and 9,410 MW by FY 2029-30, against a committed 3,000 MW by FY 2027-28 internal net-zero target and about 9,500 MW by FY 2029-30. Delivery routes are JVs with state gencos (CIL Rajasthan Akshay Urja Limited with RRVUNL, including 875 MW at Pugal Solar Park; a proposed JV with UPRVUNL in Uttar Pradesh), tariff-based competitive bidding (600 MW awarded at Jalaun Solar Park via NHPC's TBCB), captive projects and C&I supply - including MoUs with C&I consumers for 4.5 GW of renewable power through wind-solar hybrid projects, with planned development of 1.5 GW wind and 3 GW solar. Storage is a new growth area with BESPAs signed for a total of 267.5 MW / 1,070 MWh (187.5 MW/750 MWh with TGGENCO in Telangana and 80 MW/320 MWh with GRIDCO in Odisha). A wind portfolio has been initiated in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, and a dedicated Renewable Energy Division at headquarters steers the programme with CMPDIL as project management consultant. In conventional power, a 50:50 JV with Damodar Valley Corporation will develop a 2 x 800 MW (1,600 MW) brownfield thermal plant at Chandrapura with an investment of H 21,000 Crores. Capacity utilisation in FY 2025-26 was 88% for opencast and 77% for underground mines, with approximately 2,462 million cubic metres of coal and overburden handled, and 2.20 MT of washed coking coal and 6.51 MT of washed non-coking coal produced through washeries.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Large scale of operations allowing economies in scale of production - world's largest coal producer at 768.19 MT in FY 2025-26, nearly 74% of India's total coal output
- Meets about 40% of the country's primary commercial energy requirement
- Large coal resource base
- Geographical spread of operations in India allows proximity to a large and diversified customer base
- Strong financial credentials and substantial operating cash flows supporting mining investment, infrastructure, shareholder returns and strategic initiatives
- Skilled and diversified workforce with experience
- Well positioned to cater to high demand of coal in India
- Consistent track record of growth and strong track record of financial performance
- Strong capabilities for exploration, mine planning and operations, supported by in-house consultancy arm CMPDIL
- Integrated mining capabilities across the coal value chain
- Long-term demand visibility - FSA commitment for power, non-power and bridge linkage of about 793.90 MTPA as on 31.03.2026; operative SHAKTI linkage of about 643.4 MTPA with power sector and 119.2 MTPA with non-power consumers
- Quality assurance infrastructure - twelve empanelled third-party sampling agencies, auto mechanical samplers at silo loading points, live camera feed; declared-vs-analysed GCV gap of only 56.7 Kcal/kg and final grade conformity of 86% in FY 2025-26
- Digital Online Reconciliation Portal facilitating over 1,600 joint reconciliation statements, reducing disputes
- Evacuation infrastructure build-out - First Mile Connectivity projects of 432 MTY cumulative capacity operationalised
